1: Chapter 1: A Visitor on a Rainy Night

The rain in Ishikawa had been falling for three days straight. Haruka Sato's older sister had gone off to the capital in the spring, and ever since, Haruka had been running the town's little pharmacy all alone.
When night fell, she closed the shutters, counted the day's takings, blew out the lamp, and went upstairs.
No sooner had she lain down than a furious knocking came at the door below, and a man's voice called out. "Is anyone there?"

A young man stood in the doorway, soaked to the bone. Blood was seeping through the cloth wrapped around his left arm. He gave his name as Ken'ichi Mori and said he belonged to the Azure Dragon Society.
"I'd like you to see to my wound," Mori said quietly. "I'll pay. Will 3,500 yen be enough?"
Mori drew a letter wrapped in oiled paper from inside his coat. "I have to get this letter to Seifu by May 18."
Haruka sighed to herself. It was the season for buying in medicinal herbs, and she was so busy she barely had a moment to breathe.
Even so, Haruka did not take the money. "I'll take you up the mountain early tomorrow morning," she said, and nothing more.
2: As soon as day broke, the two of them set out. Haruka slung a basket on her back; inside were rice balls, medicinal herbs, and an old umbrella.

Halfway up the mountain they met an old man named Shigeru Tanaka, who was splitting firewood. He set down his axe and lowered his voice. The evening before, he said, three strangers had been going around the entrance to the town asking about a young man who had been injured.
"Haruka, take the back road," Tanaka said. "The main road isn't safe." Haruka thanked him.
The back road was narrow and slippery. Haruka went first, planting each step firmly. Mori followed in silence.

By noon the rain had stopped, and the mountain mist slowly cleared until the roof of Seifu Temple came into view in the distance. A nun stood before the gate. It was a woman named Shizuka Yamamoto, who received guests at the temple.
Yamamoto took the letter, checked the red seal on the envelope, and nodded. "The head priest has waited two years for this letter."
Mori said to Haruka, "You saved my life." Haruka laughed. "Then next time you come, fix the roof of the medicine shop," she answered. Mori stayed on at the temple.
In the evening, Haruka went down the mountain alone. By the time she reached home it was already dark; she lit the lamp and sat for a long while in the back room behind the shop counter.
